strengths: The paper addresses a practical NLP problem: adapting LLMs while producing low-bit weights without a separate high-precision LoRA inference branch. Quantizing the merged weights offers a useful alternative to QA-LoRA’s constrained adapter structure.

The evaluation covers several model families and sizes from 3B to 33B, both 3-bit and 4-bit quantization, seven commonsense tasks, and zero-/five-shot MMLU. Results generally favor L4Q, with some substantial improvements under 3-bit quantization.

The reported efficiency results support a concrete engineering contribution. For 7B models, training memory is 25.4 GB versus 79.5 GB for full QAT and 25.1 GB for ordinary LoRA. Inference measurements use the same quantized kernel for merged and unmerged models, providing useful evidence for eliminating the adapter branch.
The architectural comparison is understandable, and the appendices provide useful initialization, rank, and group-size ablations alongside detailed benchmark results.
weaknesses: Baseline fidelity is insufficiently established. Section 4.1 states that LoRA adapters use random A and zero B initialization, leaving unclear whether LoftQ retains its defining SVD-based initialization. Its near-chance 3-bit MMLU results particularly need investigation. The explicitly disclosed uniform-quantization substitutions provide controlled comparisons, but do not establish superiority over the original QLoRA and LoftQ configurations.

Training-efficiency comparisons have material confounds. Appendix D uses sequence length 128 only for 33B L4Q, versus 2048 for other configurations, limiting conclusions from its memory and training-time comparisons. L4Q also receives half the reported iterations of PTQ-based methods; a single training-loss curve does not establish comparable convergence across models. Matched workloads and validation-based stopping would strengthen these claims.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendices. The manuscript does not identify an L4Q implementation release or fully specify the custom backward implementation, microbatching, gradient accumulation, and checkpointing. The relationship between Figure 3’s 100 training steps and Appendix B’s 12,800 iterations is unclear. Table 9 also omits LoftQ and LLaMA-3 settings.

The explanation of the central mechanism needs greater precision. QAT-LoRA already optimizes quantization and adapter parameters under a shared loss; different local gradient paths do not establish that optimization is decoupled. Moreover, Eqs. 29–30 should explicitly apply the elementwise clipping mask to the weight gradient before contraction with the adapter matrices. A precise backward algorithm and controls separating learned quantization parameters, initialization, and memory management would clarify the contribution.

Many accuracy advantages are only a few tenths of a point, without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Superiority is also not universal: on 3-bit LLaMA-2 13B five-shot MMLU, L4Q scores 50.0 versus QLoRA’s 50.6 and GPTQ’s 50.4. The promising results make Findings plausible, but unresolved baseline and reproducibility concerns prevent a clear positive recommendation.
